newsitem.title: USA: Finding funds to beat the market.
newsitem.headline: Finding funds to beat the market.

text.p: Lately, few fund managers talk much about "beating the market" -- that is, delivering returns that outpace the broad market indices such as the Standard & Poor's 500.
And even fewer managers actually do it: In fact, only about a third of active money managers have outpaced the S&P 500 during the past several years.
Still, a few bold investment managers haven't given up the fight to beat the market. What's more, the best of them are likely to achieve their goal over the long term.

The failure of so many funds to keep pace with the indexes has fuelled the popularity of index funds. As the name suggests, index funds simply try to keep pace with a particular benchmark such as the S&P 500 or the Russell 2000 Index of small-company shares. Thus, they aren't likely to beat the market -- but they won't lag it by much, either.

One recent report by brokerage Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette found that some 10 percent of new money flowing into mutual funds goes to the indexers. Meanwhile, even non-index funds that purport to be actively managed have been sticking close to the shares that make up the broad indexes, for fear of being left behind if those indexes post big gains.

One result: Stocks that make up the major indexes have been buoyed by huge inflows of cash. That's one reason why shares of big blue chips such as Coca Cola Co., Intel Corp. and Microsoft Corp. have been such strong performers during the market's recent surge. Meanwhile, shares of companies that aren't included in the major indexes have been left out in the cold. As a result, many of them have stayed undervalued.

That situation creates excellent opportunities for fund managers who are still willing to do some homework to find the best bargains in the stock market. Typically, such managers spend their time poring over financial reports, talking to company management and even visiting firms to find ones whose shares are right for their portfolios. In other words, they do the old-fashioned, elemental work of stock-picking.

Some of those managers have suffered mediocre returns during the past year, because they've been unwilling to buy the most popular stocks. But over the long run their ability to spot shares that are trading at attractive prices based on companies' underlying earnings potential or other qualities should pay off with market-beating gains.

Many funds that invest in emerging companies simply buy the trendiest, hottest shares and hold on for the ride -- selling them as soon as things get bumpy. But such momentum investing isn't for Warburg Pincus managers Beth Dater and Steve Lurito. They and a team of five research analysts devote their efforts to doing company research on small and midsized firms.

Moreover, the managers don't limit themselves to a rigid set of criteria to make their choices -- and they shun the computer screening techniques that are popular at many funds these days. Instead, they consider the overall context of a company, ranging from balance sheet figures to cash flow to price/earnings ratios and the quality of management.
They do have a wish list for the companies they follow. Ideally, they'd like to see prospective three-year annual earnings growth of 20 percent or better.
They do their own earnings forecasts, rather than rely on the Wall Street consensus. They also look for low debt, typically less than 30 percent of a firm's equity.
The team also takes interest in a company's products, personnel, distribution and management style -- things that most managers today lack the time and inclination to consider.
For the moment, many investors aren't paying much attention to smaller index funds. But that will change -- perhaps the next time the stock market stumbles.

When that happens, the current market's love affair with a few hot stocks could fade quickly. Then the stock-pickers, who specialise in more stable, long-term relationships, will get the attention they deserve.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a free-lance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
